content: The available abstract excluded data from 37 women. Additionally, two groups (16 women) from a four-arm trial were excluded because those trial arms did not meet the inclusion criteria for the review. The trials contributing data to the analyses were conducted in hospital settings across various countries, including Argentina, Belgium, Denmark (four trials), Egypt (two trials), Finland, Hong Kong SAR (China), India, Israel, Italy, Malaysia (two trials), the Netherlands, Pakistan (two trials), Uganda, and the United Kingdom (four trials). The largest trial involved 13 centers across Pakistan, Uganda, and the United Kingdom. Ten trials were conducted in multiple centers within single countries, ranging from two to 11 sites, while the remaining 11 trials were conducted in single hospitals. The number of women randomized in these trials ranged from 30 to 577. Thirteen trials included only women with singleton pregnancies, while the remaining eight trials did not specify this detail. Some trials defined a minimum gestational age or range in their inclusion criteria: ≥20 weeks (one trial), ≥28 weeks (four trials), ≥34 weeks (three trials), 34–42 weeks (one trial), and ≥37 weeks (two trials). One trial included both term and preterm women, while nine trials did not report gestational age. Most trials diagnosed retained placenta 30 minutes after birth, but the timing for diagnosis varied. Two trials (73 women) diagnosed retained placenta at 15 minutes, six trials (295 women) at 20 minutes (though one of these trials administered treatment at 30 minutes), 11 trials (1,736 women) at 30 minutes, one trial (54 women) at 45 minutes, and one trial (28 women) at 60 minutes. Most trials specified a time point post-treatment (or post-diagnosis in the expectant management group) for manual removal of the placenta (MROP). MROP was performed at 15 minutes post-treatment/diagnosis in four trials (163 women), at 30 minutes in 11 trials (1,388 women), at 40 minutes in one trial (37 women), at 30–45 minutes in one trial (200 women), and at 45 minutes in one trial (81 women). In two trials (117 women), the protocol for MROP was not described. The trials in this evidence summary compared umbilical vein injection (UVI) of oxytocin solution with UVI of saline solution, plasma expander, prostaglandin solution, ergometrine solution, and carbetocin solution. In comparisons with prostaglandins and carbetocin, women receiving oxytocin were analyzed as the control group. Five trials (all oxytocin versus saline) used a placebo. All drugs were administered in saline solution, but the dose and total volume of solution varied between trials, and different types of prostaglandins were used. For UVI of oxytocin versus saline, doses ranged from 10 IU to 100 IU, with varying volumes of saline solution. For example, one trial (35 women) compared oxytocin 10 IU in 10 mL saline versus 10 mL saline alone, while another trial (577 women) compared oxytocin 50 IU in 25 mL saline versus sterile water placebo in 5 mL saline. Other trials compared oxytocin with plasma expanders, prostaglandins, ergometrine, or carbetocin, but the evidence for these comparisons was of very low certainty. Surgical interventions, including hysterectomy, were not reported as independent outcomes in the Cochrane review but were included in the reporting of severe maternal morbidity. Severe maternal morbidities were defined as hysterectomy, admission to intensive care, renal or respiratory failure, and additional surgical procedures to treat postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) other than MROP. Procedure-related complications, such as abdominal pain and hypertension following UVI of oxytocin, were unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. Similarly, the effects of UVI of oxytocin on mean blood loss, postpartum anemia, nausea, vomiting, and shivering were also uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. The Cochrane review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of oxytocin (or other uterotonics) with normal saline via UVI for the active management of the third stage of labor until new evidence becomes available. The desirable and undesirable effects of UVI of oxytocin compared to other regimens remain uncertain, and the overall certainty of the evidence is very low. The intervention requires resources such as uterotonic solutions, needles, syringes, normal saline, and gloves, which are typically available in adequately equipped hospital settings. However, resource constraints, inconsistent supplies, and concerns about oxytocin storage in areas with limited electricity may hinder its use, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Skilled health personnel are required to perform the intervention, and additional training may be necessary in settings where it is not routinely available. The World Health Organization (WHO) highlights that reducing maternal morbidity due to PPH could improve health equity, particularly for disadvantaged women in rural or low-resource settings. However, no direct evidence was identified regarding the acceptability or feasibility of UVI of oxytocin for retained placenta among women or providers. Injectable oxytocin is widely used internationally and in various resource settings, but perceptions of its use vary, particularly in LMICs, where traditional techniques and herbal medicines are sometimes preferred.
